title: MapReduce: a thousand machines, two small functions
dek: In 2004 two engineers showed that most big data jobs fit one shape: a map function, a reduce function, and a library that splits the input, moves the data between machines and re-runs whatever fails. Batch processing on thousands of machines became something any engineer could write in an afternoon.

items: You write map (turn each record into key–value pairs) and reduce (combine all the values for one key). The library runs them on thousands of machines.
Between the two sits the shuffle: every pair with the same key goes to the same reducer. That step is what makes counting, grouping and joining at scale possible.
Machines die and some are slow, so the library re-runs failed tasks and starts backup copies of the last slow ones. Without backups, a sort in the paper took 44% longer.

body.x: The paper: "MapReduce: Simplified Data Processing on Large Clusters" by Jeffrey Dean and Sanjay Ghemawat, OSDI 2004.

Building a search index takes hundreds of batch computations over terabytes: count the links to each page, group pages by site, build the word-to-page index. Each one was simple, but running it on hundreds of machines meant writing the same hard code every time: split the input, hand out work, move partial results, notice crashes, redo lost work. The paper's point was that the hard part is always the same, so it should be written once.

body.label: Orders per dish
body.x:
map(order_id, order):
    for dish in order.dishes:
        emit(dish, 1)

reduce(dish, counts):
    emit(dish, sum(counts))
body.say: Map: for each dish in an order, emit the dish and the number one. Reduce: for each dish, emit the dish and the sum of its ones.

body.x: That is a complete job: orders per dish across a whole day of Zotato logs, on as many machines as you like. The same shape builds an inverted index (map: word to page; reduce: collect the pages), counts clicks per ad, or joins two datasets on a shared key.

body.cap: Map runs where the data is and writes its pairs, bucketed by key, to local disk. Each reducer pulls its bucket from every map worker, sorts by key and adds up. Nothing in the job's code mentions machines, networks or failures.

items: The input is cut into pieces of 16 to 64 MB, and a master hands each piece to a map worker, preferably one that already stores a copy, so most input is read from local disk rather than over the network.
Each map worker splits its output into R buckets by hash(key) mod R and writes them to its own disk.
Each of the R reducers fetches its bucket from every map worker, sorts by key, and calls reduce once per key. Its output goes to the shared file system.
An optional combiner pre-adds on the map side, so a worker sends (biryani, 412) once instead of 412 copies of (biryani, 1).

body.cap: Worker 3's finished map output lived on its own disk, so losing the machine lost the output and the task runs again. Near the end, the master starts a backup of the slowest task; whichever copy finishes first is used and the other is stopped.

items: The master pings every worker. Tasks on a worker that stops answering go to others, including map tasks it had already finished.
Finished reduce tasks are not re-run: their output is already safe in the shared file system.
A few slow machines (a failing disk, a busy neighbour) can hold up a whole job. Backup copies of the last tasks cut a sort in the paper from 1,283 seconds to 891.
Re-running is safe because map and reduce have no side effects: running a task twice gives the same answer.

body.x: MapReduce and its open-source copy in Hadoop powered a decade of batch processing. Its weakness is that every step writes to disk, so a pipeline of ten jobs reads and writes the data ten times. Later engines such as Spark keep data in memory between steps and plan a whole pipeline at once, and stream processors apply the same map and group-by-key ideas to data as it arrives. The vocabulary of map, shuffle and reduce stayed.

items: For daily or hourly reports over large logs (orders per restaurant, clicks per ad, top searches), describe a batch job: read raw logs from object storage, group by key, write the results to a table. That is the batch half of the Ad clicks problem.
Name the key you group by, and watch for skew: one huge key, such as a viral ad, sends everything to one reducer. Split it into sub-keys and combine at the end.
Make jobs safe to re-run: the same input gives the same output, written to a new location and switched over when the job finishes.
If results are needed in seconds rather than hours, say so and move to stream processing.

body.label: Go deeper: numbers from the paper

body.x: Typical jobs used M = 200,000 map tasks and R = 5,000 reduce tasks on 2,000 machines. Far more tasks than machines lets the master balance the load and spread a dead machine's work across all the others. Sorting a terabyte took 891 seconds on about 1,800 machines; killing 200 of the worker processes in the middle of the run made it only 5% slower.
